notes.meaning: The tribes of Reuben and Gad owned very large flocks and herds. As they looked across the conquered areas of Jazer and Gilead east of the Jordan River, they noticed the rich green pastures were ideal for their animals. They were drawn by what looked convenient and profitable for their livestock. It is easy for worldly advantages to catch our eyes and guide our choices.

Leaders from Gad and Reuben came to Moses, Eleazar the high priest, and the chief leaders of Israel with an official request. Gad is mentioned first here, likely because their leaders spoke up first or took charge of organizing the plan. They brought their idea respectfully to the proper authorities rather than trying to seize the land on their own.

The two tribes listed several prominent cities east of the Jordan that Israel had recently conquered with God's help. They pointed out that this newly won region was perfect pastureland, and they reminded Moses that they had many animals to feed. They saw a ready-made home that was already conquered and needed no further fighting from them.

The tribes asked permission to take this eastern region as their permanent home, adding the blunt plea not to be brought across the Jordan River. Their request sounded like they wanted to settle down in comfort and leave the difficult work of taking Canaan to the rest of the nation. It showed a dangerous willingness to stop short of the actual land God had promised them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some older Catholic commentators saw this as an example of people who want the rewards of heaven without putting in the spiritual labor to run the race.

notes.meaning: Moses reacted with sharp anger and immediately challenged their motives. He asked whether it was right for them to sit at peace and enjoy their herds while the other ten tribes risked their lives in bloody warfare. God's people are called to carry burdens together, not abandon their brothers in hard times.

Moses warned them that staying behind would crush the spirit and courage of the other tribes. If two entire tribes dropped out of the army, the rest of Israel might feel abandoned and refuse to cross the river into the land God gave them. Selfish choices by a few can quickly spread fear and doubt across an entire community.

Moses reminded them of the tragedy at Kadesh-barnea forty years earlier, when twelve scouts were sent to explore the land. Ten of those scouts came back from the Valley of Eshcol with a fearful report that discouraged the whole nation from going in. Moses feared that Reuben and Gad were repeating that exact same sin by disheartening God's people.

Moses recounted how God's anger burned against the people because of their unbelief. The LORD swore a solemn oath that no adult twenty years or older who left Egypt would live to see the promised land. Their refusal to trust God and follow Him wholeheartedly brought a severe and lasting judgment.

Only Joshua and Caleb were spared from that sentence because they remained completely faithful to the LORD. They trusted God's power when everyone else gave in to fear. Caleb is called the Kenizzite, likely referring to his family line through his ancestor Kenaz.

Because of their rebellion, God made Israel wander in the barren wilderness for forty full years. The entire older generation that had done evil had to die out before the nation could move forward. Unbelief and complaining can delay the blessings God wants to give His people.

Moses bluntly called the two tribes a brood of sinners who were stepping into their fathers' footsteps. He warned that their selfish desire was about to pile even more wrath on Israel, rekindling God's fierce anger against the entire camp. Following the bad patterns of past generations only multiplies guilt.

Moses explained that if they turned away from obeying God, the LORD would leave the whole camp stranded in the desert once more. In that case, Reuben and Gad would be directly responsible for destroying the entire nation. Leading others away from God's path brings terrible harm to everyone around us.

The leaders of Reuben and Gad came back to Moses with a clear and humble compromise. They proposed to quickly repair stone pens for their flocks and rebuild the fortified cities to house their families. They took Moses' sharp warning to heart and looked for a way to serve both their households and their nation.

They promised to take up weapons and march on the front lines to help conquer Canaan until all the tribes were safely settled. Meanwhile, their wives, children, and vulnerable relatives would remain behind in fortified towns to protect them from local enemies. They planned to leave behind enough men to guard the families while sending their best fighters across the river.

They gave their word that their soldiers would not return home until every other Israelite family had received their portion of the land. They were ready to endure years of campaigning alongside their brothers. True loyalty means finishing the job rather than quitting when our own needs are met.

The two tribes confirmed that they would not ask for any land on the western side of the Jordan River. They were entirely satisfied to take their inheritance on the east side and leave all of Canaan to the other tribes. They wanted to assure Moses that their offer was sincere and that they were not trying to claim a double share.

Moses accepted their proposal on the strict condition that they go into battle before the LORD. This meant marching before the ark of the covenant, which represented God's presence among them, and staying in the fight until God drove out every enemy. Moses reminded them that the conquest was God's sacred work, not merely a military favor to their brothers.
